lesson.title: What makes a choice the best?
lesson.subtitle: Options, limits and a goal, and why allowed isn’t best

video.title: What makes a choice the best?
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello — primary teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: A quick rule and a better plan
Everywhere at school, and the lab

scenes.visual: Amina at the board after school: five outing ideas, each with a price, and a small cash box labelled 1,200.
scenes.animation: Ideas write themselves on the board one by one; the cash box pops in; a question mark appears.
scenes.narration: This term, my class has twelve hundred coins for outings, and five ideas on the board. The zoo is the favourite, but it’s also the dearest. How do I choose the best plan?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the Optimization track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: What makes a choice the best?
scenes.narration: Today: what makes a choice the best, and how to see it clearly.

scenes.visual: Three icon cards appear in a row: a list, a padlock, a target.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in as each part is named.
scenes.narration: Every decision like this has three parts. The options: what you can choose. The limits: what every plan must keep. And the goal: what “best” means, one number to make as big or as small as possible.

scenes.visual: The board again: five outings with cost and votes; the cash box; a star beside the votes.
scenes.animation: Each row lights up as it is named.
scenes.narration: For Amina, the options are the five outings. The limit is the money: twelve hundred coins. The goal is the most pupils’ votes, because the class voted for what they want.

scenes.visual: Two columns: many small ticked plans on the left; one plan with a gold star on the right.
scenes.animation: Ticks pop on the left; the star lands on the right.
scenes.narration: A plan that keeps every limit is called feasible. There are usually many feasible plans. The best feasible plan, the one with the best score on the goal, is called optimal.

scenes.visual: Two outing cards slide into a basket: the zoo, then the museum; the total appears.
scenes.animation: Cards chain with arrows; the total counts up.
scenes.narration: Amina tries the obvious rule: favourite first. The zoo, seven hundred coins and twenty-five votes, then the museum, five hundred coins and eighteen votes. That’s all twelve hundred coins, and forty-three votes.

scenes.visual: Two columns: favourite first (43 votes) against a better mix (45 votes).
scenes.animation: The right column fills in item by item; its total glows.
scenes.narration: But the museum, the farm and the river park also cost twelve hundred coins, and win forty-five votes. Three smaller outings beat one big favourite. Checking a plan is easy: just add it up. Finding the best is the hard part.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma with a clipboard: a plan with three ticks. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! My plan keeps every limit: the budget, the dates, the seats on the bus. What does that tell me?

scenes.visual: The answer card ‘Feasible, maybe not best’ gets a check. Beside it, a small grid of 32 plans, then a huge cloud of plans.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; the grid fills; the cloud grows past the frame.
scenes.narration: It’s feasible: allowed, but not yet the best. To know it’s optimal, you compare it with every other plan, or use a method that is sure. With five outings there are only thirty-two plans to check. With thirty choices there are over a billion.

scenes.visual: Four small scenes: a timetable grid, an exam hall, a bus on a village road, a lunch plate.
scenes.animation: Each scene slides in as it is named.
scenes.narration: You meet these problems all over school. The timetable: periods and teachers, with no clashes. Exam week: no pupil in two exams at once. The bus round: every village, the shortest drive. And lunch: enough food, for the least money.

scenes.visual: A phone with the lab: six loads as tiles, a truck with a weight bar, a points counter.
scenes.animation: A finger taps loads onto the truck; the weight bar fills.
scenes.narration: In the app, pack a truck for a village school. Each load has a weight and points for how much the school needs it, and the truck takes a thousand kilos. Try your own load first, then compare it with the best.

scenes.visual: Amina holds up the class vote sheet. Three answer cards appear beside her.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A colleague says the best plan always starts with the class favourite. Is she right?

scenes.visual: The answer card gets the check; four summary lines and a takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: Not always: three smaller outings won more votes than the zoo. Remember: name the options, the limits and the goal. A feasible plan keeps every limit; the optimal one is the best of them. And check a quick rule before you trust it.

scenes.visual: Amina’s class in groups with cards on desks: costs, votes and a budget line on the board.
scenes.animation: Cards move between piles; one group raises its hand.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: plan the class outings together. Write five ideas with their costs, and let pupils vote. Then groups find the mix with the most votes inside the budget. Ask them: whose favourite was left out, and what would be fair next term?

checkpoints.prompt: A plan keeps every limit. What does that tell you?

options.text: It is feasible: allowed, maybe not the best

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — keeping every limit makes a plan feasible. Only comparing it with the others shows whether it’s the best.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a plan that keeps every limit is feasible: allowed. Other feasible plans may score better on the goal.

checkpoints.prompt: Does the best plan always start with the favourite?

options.text: Yes: the favourite belongs in every best plan
No: a mix of smaller choices can score more
Only when the favourite is the cheapest

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the museum, the farm and the river park won 45 votes, more than the zoo and the museum’s 43.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — favourite first gave 43 votes, but three smaller outings won 45 for the same money.
